Suspected  extremists killed two Naga civilians in Manipur’s Senapati district on Saturday, barely 48 hours  after  Myanmar- based assailants gunned down four persons in Kam- jong district, a district oﬃ- cial said, adding that two more persons were injured in the incident. The oﬃcial could not conﬁrm how the two Naga men, identiﬁed as Rocky Mao of Chowainamei vil- lage and Kumar Poumai of Laii Shiraﬁi village, were killed or what led to the in- cident. Senapati is a Naga- dominated district. One of

the deceased is a Mao Naga and the other is a Poumai Naga. The two injured, Ashiho Sani and Adani Ma- nio, belong to the Mao Na- ga community. The  injured  were rushed to a private hospital for treatment, while the bodies of the deceased were taken to Senapati Dis- trict Hospital for autopsy and other legal formalities, an oﬃcial said.

Manipur Chief Minister Yumnam  Khemchand Singh, who was in Senapati district on an oﬃcial visit when reports of the inci- dent came in, strongly con- demned the killings and called them a “cowardly act of violence”.  Former Chief Minister N. Biren Singh also con- demned the killings and said there had been more than 60 murders this year. In a post on X, Mr. Biren Singh said, “The killings are a matter of grave con- cern. Armed militants en- tered their homes and shot them dead while they were asleep. These were civi- lians who deserved to live without fear.”
Two persons were also injured in the mishap that took place 48 hours after four persons were killed in Kamjong

he Election Com- mission (EC) on Sa- turday announced a slew of measures ad- dressing concerns over the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls across the country, in- cluding stopping physical hearings for unmapped vo- ters or those with logical discrepancies in their en- umeration forms. It said that the declara- tion accompanying Form 6 (used for fresh voter regis- tration) is mandatory only during the current SIR pro- cess. This in eﬀect means that new voters who seek inclusion in electoral rolls after the ongoing SIR need not  submit  any  such declaration. The Election Commis-

sion also said that any per- son whose name has got left out during SIR or the- reafter, and any person in- cluding young/ ﬁrst-time voters, may apply to the electoral registration oﬃc- er (ERO) concerned, for in- clusion of their names in the electoral rolls.  A special drive will im-

mediately be launched for their enrolment, it said in a press note. The SIR process has al- ready been completed in 20  States  and  Union Territories. The fresh initiatives of the poll body came after a meeting of the full bench of the commission on Sa-
turday afternoon and days after reports emerged of a rift within the Election Commissioners over these and other issues in the SIR process as well as the inter- nal working of the EC.
‘Complete approval’ The Election Commission’s press note was pertinently
accompanied by a photo- graph of all the three Elec- tion Commissioners and mentioned that it “has the approval  of  the  full commission”.
EC switches to damage control mode after facing ﬂak over SIR

Delivering India’s National Statement at the UN Gener- al Assembly, External Af- fairs  Minister S. Jaishankar on Saturday said the coun- try will exercise its right to defend itself against terro- rism while focusing on the impact of conﬂicts on the Global South.  In a response to Pakis- tan Prime Minister Sheh- baz Sharif’s speech a day before, where he had criti- cised India for launching Operation  Sindoor  last year, Mr. Jaishankar said that there could be “no di- lution” of the world’s zero- tolerance approach to ter- rorism. “Yesterday, a serial practitioner of terrorism misrepresented facts be- fore this Assembly. Argu- ments were invoked to nor- malise terrorism and claim immunity from its conse- quences,” Mr. Jaishankar said, attacking Mr. Sharif’s speech, in which he had called Kashmir the “jugu-

lar vein” of Pakistan and accused India of human rights violations in the re- gion. Mr. Sharif had also claimed that the BJP go- vernment in India un- leashed a “reign of terror” against minorities in the country.  “Our right to defend ourselves against terrorism will be exercised,” Mr. Jaishankar said, adding that governments indulg- ing in state-sponsored ter- rorism with a “cross-bor- der purpose” must be held to account.

n artiﬁcial intelligence (AI)-enabled enforcement camera, installed to detect traﬃc violations in Bengaluru, recently issued a routine helmet violation challan to a not-so-routine defaulter: a guitar case riding on its owner’s back. Souvik Dutta was travelling on his scooter from Hebbal towards Tin
Factory with a guitar strapped to his back. The camera apparently

mistook the guitar case for a pillion rider and wrongly identiﬁed it as a person travelling without a helmet. A challan, along with a photograph captured by the camera, was subsequently sent to Mr. Dutta’s wife, who owns the scooter.
Limitations of system The incident has drawn attention to the limitations of automated traﬃc enforcement systems. A senior traﬃc police oﬃcer

admitted that the reported violation by the ‘pillion rider’ was a ‘false ﬂag’, caused by an error in judgment by the AI system, which happens occasionally.  Noting that the system has yet to achieve 100% accuracy, the oﬃcer said that such violations can be questioned, following which they are veriﬁed and rectiﬁed.

Reign continues:  The Indian kabaddi teams maintained their supremacy by retaining the men’s and women’s titles at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya on Saturday. The men defeated Iran 40-34 and the women pipped the  same opponent 37-34 in the ﬁnals.  R.V. MOORTHY (REPORT: PAGE 15)

At least 27 questions in this year’s Civil Services Exami- nation  (CSE)  Prelims, across general studies and aptitude  papers,  have come under dispute, with candidates claiming that the answers in the provi- sional answer key released by the Union Public Ser- vice Commission (UPSC) are either incorrect, have no correct answer, or allow more than one possible answer.  At least two groups of aspirants have challenged the questions. The cases
are being heard by the Central Administrative Tri- bunal.  One group of four candi- dates has challenged eight questions, while another group of 63 aspirants has challenged 27 questions,

including the eight chal- lenged in the ﬁrst petition. The  candidates  argued that many of them missed the cut-oﬀ for the Mains ex- amination by only a few marks. The aspirants, who did not wish to be identi- ﬁed, said that a disputed answer is rarely just about one question, as it can ren- der a candidate ineligible for the Mains examination, cost them an entire year of preparation and, for those appearing in their ﬁnal at- tempt, end their chances of qualifying.
